newsitem.title: USA: Venezuela to start talks on new IMF program - Matos.
newsitem.headline: Venezuela to start talks on new IMF program - Matos.

text.p: Venezuela will start talks with the International Monetary Fund on a new program after the IMF/World Bank spring meeting, Venezuelan Finance Minister Luis Raul Matos Azocar said on Sunday.

"Once this event is over we will come to the Fund to talk about extending our current standby program or switching to a 'shadow' program. Whichever way we go, we will continue in close cooperation with the IMF," Matos, who is attending the spring meeting, told reporters.

Matos said that a new standby program to replace the one-year deal that expires in July would have to include targets and deadlines for reforms requiring congressional approval, such as amending labor laws or the judicial system.
A "shadow" program, on the other hand, would only entail close IMF scrutiny of Venezuela's macroeconomic performance.
"And for a government (as President Rafael Caldera's) which does not have a majority in Congress, that is an important factor to be taken into account," Matos said.
Either way, he further argued, Venezuela would not need to tap the IMF for financing.
Venezuela's foreign reserves were bolstered last year by the rise in oil prices, allowing Caldera's government to waive the remaining tranches of a $1.2 billion IMF loan.
However, the Venezuelan government plans to use resources from that windfall to raise public sector wages, a decision that will push up inflation.
Matos said the impact of the wage increases would start to be noticed in May but argued that it would be "temporary".
He stressed that the IMF was in full agreement with Venezuela's inflation target of about 30 percent for 1997, down from nearly 100 percent in 1996.
Seeking to clear up confusion about the IMF's projections for Venezuela's inflation, Matos said his government's target refers to year-on-year inflation rather than a 12-month average.
The IMF used the latter methodology in its World Economic Outlook report issued last week, showing it expected a 46.6 percent increase in consumer prices for 1997.
An IMF spokesman later concurred with Matos, saying the year-on-year calculation was the one used for setting inflation targets in their programs.
Venezuela is also trying to smoothe out payments on up to $25 billion of its commercial debt, which are front-loaded for 1998 and 1999.
Matos said the government was studying proposals put forward last month by 20 investment banks and expected to make a decision sometime in May.
"It could happen early in May but we want to give ourselves time until the end of the month. We don't want bankers to swamp us with calls to find out whether they've won," he said.

Under current terms, Venezuela would have to pay about $3.0 billion, or 40 percent of the government's ordinary revenue, every year through 1999 to service the outstanding debt. Venezuela would like to bring down payments to about 25 percent.
